title: The Untold Emotional Pain Behind Rachel Dying on the Journey
paragraphs: The Untold Emotional Pain Behind Rachel Dying on the Journey
Some deaths happen quietly.
Not because they are small.
But because heaven itself struggles to put words around the weight of what just happened.
Rachel’s death was one of those moments.
Most people remember it as a tragic Bible event tucked into a genealogy timeline. A woman dies giving birth. A husband buries her beside the road. The journey continues.
But if you slow down long enough to actually feel the scene… it becomes one of the most emotionally devastating moments in all of Scripture.
Because Rachel did not die in peace inside a home. She did not die surrounded by safety. She did not die after finally enjoying the life she suffered years to obtain.
She died on the road. Still traveling. Still unfinished. Still carrying promises she would never personally experience.
And millions of people silently understand that kind of pain.
The pain of finally reaching the season you prayed for… only to collapse emotionally while trying to hold it together.
The pain of carrying everyone else’s expectations while your own soul quietly bleeds underneath.
The pain of arriving at answered prayer while simultaneously losing strength to enjoy it.
This story is not just about Rachel.
It is about exhausted people who kept moving while dying internally.
It is about believers who smiled publicly while silently asking God why their journey became so heavy.
And hidden inside the Hebrew text is emotional depth most people never notice.
Genesis 35:16 says:
“Then they journeyed from Bethel. And when there was but a little distance to go to Ephrath, Rachel travailed, and she had hard labor.”
The Hebrew phrase for “hard labor” is:
קְשֹׁתָהּ בְּלִדְתָּהּ (Qeshoṯah Belidtah)
It carries the idea of severe difficulty, cruelty, intense suffering, unbearable pressure.
This was not ordinary pain.
This was overwhelming agony.
The kind of agony where breathing itself feels like warfare.
And what destroys me emotionally about this moment…
…is that Rachel had spent years crying for children.
Years.
Genesis 30:1 records her heartbreaking words to Jacob:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
In Hebrew:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי (Havah-li banim ve’im-ayin metah anokhi)
“Give me sons — if not, I am dying.”
Notice something terrifying.
The woman who emotionally said she would die without children… eventually dies while bringing forth a child.
Scripture is brutally honest.
Sometimes the thing we beg God for comes wrapped in pain we never anticipated.
Sometimes answered prayers arrive carrying weight we were never emotionally prepared to survive.
That does not mean God is cruel.
It means human beings often romanticize destinations while underestimating the suffering attached to purpose.
Rachel desperately wanted motherhood.
But motherhood did not remove sorrow from her life.
And if we are honest… many people today understand this exact emotional contradiction.
The marriage came. But so did loneliness.
The ministry grew. But exhaustion quietly grew with it.
The business succeeded. But anxiety followed every achievement.
The baby arrived. But postpartum darkness entered the room too.
The platform expanded. But private emptiness became unbearable.
People think blessing automatically removes struggle.
Rachel’s story destroys that illusion.
Sometimes blessings and breaking happen in the same season.
And that truth makes many believers uncomfortable.
Because we secretly thought obedience would protect us from emotional devastation.
But Scripture never promised a painless journey.
In fact, some of God’s most loved servants suffered deeply while still walking inside divine purpose.
Rachel’s death happened while Jacob’s family was moving toward destiny.
That detail matters.
Because many Christians mistakenly assume hardship means they left God’s will.
Not always.
Sometimes you are hurting precisely because you are still moving.
The text says they were close to Ephrath. Close.
The Hebrew wording implies nearness. They were almost there.
And isn’t that emotionally familiar?
Some of the deepest breakdowns happen when people are almost at the next chapter.
Right before breakthrough. Right before healing. Right before stability. Right before rest.
The enemy loves attacking exhausted people near transition.
Rachel was physically depleted. Emotionally strained. Travel-worn. And now labor contractions violently overtook her body.
Then comes one of the saddest verses in Genesis.
Genesis 35:17:
“And it came to pass, when she was in hard labor, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also.”
The Hebrew phrase:
אַל־תִּירְאִי (Al-Tira’i)
Means: “Do not fear.”
But think about this carefully.
Why would the midwife say “do not fear” unless Rachel herself was terrified?
This was not calm surrender.
This was panic.
This was a woman sensing death approaching.
A woman realizing she might not survive this moment.
And suddenly the story becomes painfully human.
Rachel is not merely a Bible character anymore.
She becomes every exhausted mother. Every emotionally overwhelmed believer. Every person who silently wondered if they could survive the pressure crushing them.
Some of you reading this know exactly what that feels like.
You kept showing up. Kept praying. Kept serving. Kept carrying responsibilities.
While internally thinking: “I don’t know how much more of this I can endure.”
And maybe nobody around you fully noticed.
Because wounded people often become experts at appearing functional.
Then Scripture delivers a sentence that emotionally shatters me every single time I read it.
Genesis 35:18:
“And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing…”
The Hebrew says:
בְּצֵאת נַפְשָׁהּ (Be-tzet nafshah)
“As her soul was going out.”
This language is deeply intimate.
The Bible does not merely say she died.
It describes her soul departing.
The Hebrew word:
נֶפֶשׁ (Nephesh)
Can mean soul, life, inner self, living being, breath, emotional essence.
Scripture slows down the moment intentionally.
As if heaven itself pauses beside this dying woman.
And during her final breaths… Rachel names the child:
בֶּן־אוֹנִי (Ben-Oni)
Meaning: “Son of my sorrow.” “Son of my affliction.” “Son of my pain.”
Can you feel the emotional gravity of that?
Her last act on earth was naming her pain.
Not hiding it. Not masking it. Not pretending strength.
She verbalized the sorrow.
And there are people reading this right now who have been carrying silent grief for years because church culture taught them to suppress emotional honesty.
But Rachel teaches us something important.
Acknowledging pain is not rebellion against God.
Pretending pain does not exist helps nobody.
Even Jesus openly wept.
In Greek, John 11:35 says:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς (edakrysen ho Iēsous)
“Jesus wept.”
Not performed. Not symbolically. Not emotionally detached.
He wept.
The Son of God Himself publicly entered grief.
So why do modern believers think emotional suppression equals holiness?
Rachel’s dying words expose a truth many Christians avoid:
People can deeply love God and still experience devastating emotional pain.
Then Jacob does something remarkable.
Genesis 35:18 continues:
“But his father called him Benjamin.”
In Hebrew:
בִּנְיָמִין (Binyamin)
Meaning: “Son of the right hand.” “Son of favor.” “Son of strength.”
Rachel named him from pain. Jacob renamed him through covenant identity.
This is one of the most beautiful emotional pictures of redemption in all of Scripture.
Because grief tried to define the child.
But destiny had another name.
And maybe this is where some of you need to breathe again.
Because your trauma is not your final identity.
Your depression is not your final name.
Your failure is not your final name.
Your addiction is not your final name.
Your shame is not your final name.
Your worst moment does not have authority to permanently define what God can redeem.
Jesus specializes in renaming broken stories.
Simon became Peter. Saul became Paul. Abram became Abraham.
God repeatedly rewrites identities.
And maybe you have spent years calling yourself what pain named you.
Unwanted. Dirty. Too broken. Too late. Unlovable. Damaged. Disqualified.
But heaven speaks differently.
Isaiah 62:2 says:
“And thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name.”
God renames people grace restores.
But there is still another heartbreaking layer inside Rachel’s story.
She was buried beside the road.
Genesis 35:19:
“So Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath.”
In the way.
On the journey.
Not at the destination.
And that reality hurts because many people expected life to finally become easier once they reached certain milestones.
Yet some seasons feel like endless movement without emotional arrival.
Always carrying. Always enduring. Always sacrificing. Always surviving.
Some of you are spiritually exhausted because your entire life has felt like one long road.
And maybe you secretly wonder if God still sees you there.
He does.
The Gospel is full of God meeting weary people on roads.
The Emmaus road. The Damascus road. The Jericho road.
Even Jesus carried His cross along a road toward Golgotha.
Christianity is not built around untouched people living painless lives.
It is built around a suffering Savior who entered human agony personally.
Isaiah 53:3 calls Him:
“A man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
In Hebrew:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי (Ish mak’ovot veyadua choli)
A man intimately familiar with suffering.
Jesus understands emotional pain from the inside.
Betrayal. Rejection. Abandonment. Grief. Exhaustion. Mockery. Loneliness.
This is why the Gospel matters so deeply.
Because Christianity is not God observing pain from a distance.
It is God entering pain Himself.
And maybe somebody reading this has been silently falling apart lately.
You still function. Still smile. Still attend church. Still answer messages. Still post online.
But deep down you are tired.
Tired of carrying invisible burdens. Tired of pretending strength. Tired of feeling emotionally stranded in the middle of your journey.
Rachel’s story reminds us that God sees exhausted travelers too.
Not just victorious people.
Not just strong people.
Not just emotionally polished believers.
He sees weary souls.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The Lord is near unto them that are of a broken heart.”
The Hebrew word for broken:
נִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב (Nishberei-lev)
Means shattered-hearted. Crushed internally.
God draws near to shattered people.
Not away from them.
And if you have secretly been losing emotional strength lately… hear this clearly:
You are not weak because the journey became painful.
Even faithful people bleed.
Even obedient people cry.
Even chosen people collapse emotionally sometimes.
Rachel’s death on the journey was tragic.
But it was not meaningless.
Because centuries later… another Son would arrive through another painful journey.
Jesus Christ.
And unlike Rachel, Jesus willingly stepped into death so others could live.
The cross was not accidental.
It was love absorbing judgment. Grace carrying sin. Mercy entering suffering.
In Aramaic, one of Jesus’ cries from the cross was:
ܐܝܠ ܐܝܠ ܠܡܢܐ ܫܒܩܬܢܝ (Eli, Eli, lama shbaqtani)
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Jesus entered the deepest human anguish imaginable.
So no broken believer could ever honestly say: “God does not understand suffering.”
He understands it completely.
And because He rose again, pain is never the final chapter for those who belong to Him.
That is the hope Rachel’s story whispers through tears.
The road is painful.
But resurrection still exists.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Some people are still walking forward while quietly bleeding inside.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Nasasabi Tungkol sa Matinding Emosyonal na Sakit ni Rachel Habang Namatay sa Paglalakbay
May mga pagkamatay na tahimik.
Hindi dahil maliit ang sakit.
Kundi dahil kahit ang langit parang nahihirapang ilarawan kung gaano kabigat ang nangyari.
Isa doon ang pagkamatay ni Rachel.
Karamihan sa mga tao, nababasa lang ito bilang maikling bahagi ng kasaysayan sa Biblia. Isang babae ang namatay habang nanganganak. Inilibing siya sa tabi ng daan. Nagpatuloy ang paglalakbay.
Pero kapag pinabagal mo ang pagbabasa… kapag hinayaan mong maramdaman mo talaga ang eksena…
Biglang nagiging isa ito sa pinaka-masakit na tagpo sa buong Kasulatan.
Dahil si Rachel ay hindi namatay sa loob ng bahay. Hindi siya namatay sa ligtas na lugar. Hindi siya namatay pagkatapos niyang tuluyang ma-enjoy ang buhay na matagal niyang ipinaglaban.
Namatay siya habang nasa daan. Habang naglalakbay. Habang hindi pa tapos ang kuwento. Habang dala-dala pa rin ang mga pangakong hindi na niya personal na makikita.
At maraming tao ngayon ang tahimik na nakakarelate sa ganoong klaseng sakit.
Yung pakiramdam na finally dumating na ang ipinagdasal mo… pero ikaw mismo, unti-unti nang nauubos.
Yung pakiramdam na pinapasan mo ang expectations ng lahat habang tahimik na dumudugo ang kaluluwa mo.
Yung sakit na natanggap mo na ang blessing… pero nawawala na ang lakas mong i-enjoy ito.
Hindi lang ito kuwento tungkol kay Rachel.
Kuwento ito ng mga taong pagod na pero tuloy pa rin ang lakad.
Mga taong nakangiti sa harap ng iba habang tahimik na nagtatanong sa Diyos: “Lord… bakit parang sobrang bigat na ng journey?”
At sa orihinal na Hebrew text, may emosyonal na lalim na kadalasang hindi napapansin.
Genesis 35:16:
“Then they journeyed from Bethel. And when there was but a little distance to go to Ephrath, Rachel travailed, and she had hard labor.”
Ang Hebrew phrase para sa “hard labor” ay:
קְשֹׁתָהּ בְּלִדְתָּהּ (Qeshoṯah Belidtah)
Ibig sabihin nito: matinding paghihirap, malupit na sakit, halos hindi na kayaning pressure.
Hindi ito ordinaryong sakit.
Ito yung klaseng sakit na parang pati paghinga mo… laban.
At ang mas masakit dito…
…si Rachel ay matagal nang umiiyak para magkaroon ng anak.
Taon.
Genesis 30:1:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
Sa Hebrew:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי (Havah-li banim ve’im-ayin metah anokhi)
“Bigyan mo ako ng mga anak… kung wala, para na rin akong mamamatay.”
Napansin mo ba?
Yung babaeng nagsabing mamamatay siya kapag hindi nagkaanak…
…sa huli, namatay habang nanganganak.
Napaka-honest ng Biblia.
Minsan ang mga bagay na matagal nating ipinagdarasal… may kasamang sakit na hindi natin inaasahan.
Minsan ang answered prayer may kasamang pressure na hindi natin kayang kontrolin.
Hindi ibig sabihin nun malupit ang Diyos.
Ibig sabihin lang… madalas romanticized ang iniisip nating blessing, pero hindi natin naiintindihan ang bigat ng purpose.
Gustong-gusto ni Rachel maging ina.
Pero hindi ibig sabihin nawala lahat ng sakit sa buhay niya.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… maraming tao ngayon ang nakakaramdam niyan.
Dumating nga ang marriage. Pero dumating din ang loneliness.
Lumago ang ministry. Pero kasabay nun, burnout.
Dumating ang baby. Pero kasama rin ang postpartum darkness.
Lumaki ang business. Pero lumala rin ang anxiety.
Dumami ang followers. Pero lalo ring naging empty sa loob.
Akala kasi ng marami, kapag blessed ka… wala ka nang struggle.
Sinisira ng kuwento ni Rachel ang maling paniniwalang iyon.
Minsan sabay dumarating ang blessing at breaking.
At uncomfortable iyon para sa maraming believers.
Kasi secretly… akala natin kapag sumusunod tayo sa Diyos, magiging madali na lahat.
Pero hindi kailanman nangako ang Diyos ng painless journey.
Sa katunayan, marami sa mga pinakamamahal ng Diyos sa Biblia ang dumanas ng matinding emotional pain.
At nangyari ang pagkamatay ni Rachel habang papunta sila sa destiny.
Mahalagang detalye iyon.
Kasi maraming Kristiyano iniisip na kapag nahihirapan sila, ibig sabihin wala na sila sa will ng Diyos.
Hindi palagi.
Minsan nasasaktan ka dahil nagpapatuloy ka pa rin.
Sabi ng text, malapit na sila sa Ephrath. Malapit na.
At hindi ba parang pamilyar iyon?
Minsan ang pinakamalalaking breakdown nangyayari kapag malapit ka na sa breakthrough.
Malapit na sa healing. Malapit na sa bagong chapter. Malapit na sa kapayapaan.
Mahilig umatake ang kaaway kapag pagod na pagod na ang tao.
Pagod na si Rachel. Pagod sa biyahe. Pagod sa katawan. Pagod emotionally.
Tapos biglang dumating ang matinding labor pain.
Pagkatapos, isa sa pinaka-masakit na verses sa Genesis.
Genesis 35:17:
“And it came to pass, when she was in hard labor, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also.”
Ang Hebrew phrase:
אַל־תִּירְאִי (Al-Tira’i)
Ibig sabihin: “Huwag kang matakot.”
Pero isipin mo ito.
Bakit sasabihin ng komadrona na “huwag kang matakot” kung hindi natatakot si Rachel?
Hindi ito calm surrender.
Ito ay panic.
Ito yung pakiramdam na alam mong may mali.
Yung pakiramdam na baka hindi ka na makaligtas.
At biglang nagiging sobrang human ng kuwento.
Si Rachel hindi na lang Bible character.
Nagiging representasyon siya ng bawat nanay na pagod. Bawat believer na emotionally overwhelmed. Bawat taong tahimik na nagtatanong: “Kaya ko pa ba talaga?”
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na alam na alam ang pakiramdam na iyon.
Tuloy lang sa trabaho. Tuloy lang sa ministry. Tuloy lang sa responsibilities. Tuloy lang sa pagngiti.
Pero sa loob-loob mo: “Pagod na pagod na ako.”
At baka wala talagang nakakapansin.
Kasi maraming sugatang tao… eksperto nang magmukhang okay.
Pagkatapos, dumating ang verse na talagang dumudurog sa puso.
Genesis 35:18:
“And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing…”
Sa Hebrew:
בְּצֵאת נַפְשָׁהּ (Be-tzet nafshah)
“Habang lumalabas ang kanyang kaluluwa.”
Napaka-intimate ng wording.
Hindi lang sinabi ng Biblia na namatay siya.
Parang pinabagal ng langit ang eksena.
Pinakita ang kaluluwa niyang unti-unting umaalis.
Ang Hebrew word na:
נֶפֶשׁ (Nephesh)
Ay maaaring ibig sabihin: kaluluwa, hininga, buhay, inner self, emotional essence.
At habang nalalapit siya sa kamatayan… pinangalanan niya ang bata:
בֶּן־אוֹנִי (Ben-Oni)
Ibig sabihin: “Anak ng aking kalungkutan.” “Anak ng aking sakit.”
Grabe iyon.
Ang huling ginawa ni Rachel sa mundo… ay pangalanan ang sakit niya.
Hindi niya itinago. Hindi niya pineke ang lakas.
At may mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na matagal nang nagtatago ng emotional pain dahil feeling nila bawal maging honest sa church.
Pero may itinuturo si Rachel.
Hindi kasalanan ang umamin na nasasaktan ka.
Maging si Jesus mismo umiyak.
John 11:35 sa Greek:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς (edakrysen ho Iēsous)
“Jesus wept.”
Hindi performance. Hindi drama.
Tunay na pag-iyak.
Kung ang Anak ng Diyos mismo umiyak… bakit maraming believers ang iniisip na bawal masaktan?
Ipinapakita ng kuwento ni Rachel na pwedeng mahal mo ang Diyos… at nasasaktan ka pa rin nang malalim.
Pero pagkatapos, may napakagandang ginawa si Jacob.
Genesis 35:18:
“But his father called him Benjamin.”
Sa Hebrew:
בִּנְיָמִין (Binyamin)
Ibig sabihin: “Anak ng kanang kamay.” “Anak ng pabor.” “Anak ng lakas.”
Pinangalanan siya ni Rachel mula sa sakit.
Pero ni-rename siya ni Jacob ayon sa covenant identity.
Napakagandang larawan nito ng redemption.
Sinubukan ng grief na pangalanan ang bata.
Pero may ibang pangalan ang destiny.
At baka may kailangang makarinig nito ngayon.
Hindi ikaw ang pangalan na ibinigay ng trauma mo.
Hindi ikaw ang addiction mo. Hindi ikaw ang shame mo. Hindi ikaw ang depression mo. Hindi ikaw ang worst mistake mo.
Marunong magbigay ng bagong pangalan ang Diyos.
Simon became Peter. Saul became Paul. Abram became Abraham.
Paulit-ulit nire-rewrite ng Diyos ang identity ng tao.
At baka matagal mo nang tinatawag ang sarili mo base sa sakit.
“Walang kwenta.” “Madumi.” “Hindi na maaayos.” “Hindi lovable.”
Pero iba ang tawag ng langit sa’yo.
Isaiah 62:2:
“And thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name.”
May bagong pangalan ang biyaya ng Diyos para sa mga taong akala nilang tapos na sila.
Pero may isa pang masakit na detalye.
Inilibing si Rachel sa tabi ng daan.
Genesis 35:19:
“So Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath.”
“In the way.”
Habang nasa journey.
Hindi pa sa destination.
At masakit iyon.
Kasi maraming tao ang umaasang gagaan ang buhay kapag narating na nila ang next chapter.
Pero minsan parang tuloy-tuloy lang ang laban.
Laging may pasan. Laging may pressure. Laging may pagod.
At baka may mga taong nagbabasa nito na emotionally exhausted na.
Pakiramdam mo buong buhay mo… puro biyahe.
At baka iniisip mo: “Lord… nakikita Mo pa ba ako?”
Oo.
Buong Gospel puno ng Diyos na sumasalubong sa pagod na tao habang nasa daan.
The Emmaus road. The Damascus road. The Jericho road.
Maging si Jesus dinala ang krus habang naglalakad papuntang Golgotha.
Ang Christianity hindi tungkol sa mga taong hindi nasasaktan.
Ito ay tungkol sa Tagapagligtas na piniling pasukin mismo ang sakit ng tao.
Isaiah 53:3:
“A man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
Sa Hebrew:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי (Ish mak’ovot veyadua choli)
Isang taong lubos na pamilyar sa paghihirap.
Alam ni Jesus ang betrayal. Alam Niya ang rejection. Alam Niya ang loneliness. Alam Niya ang exhaustion.
Kaya napakahalaga ng Gospel.
Dahil hindi lang minamasdan ng Diyos ang pain mo mula sa malayo.
Pinasok Niya ito mismo.
At baka may taong tahimik nang bumabagsak emotionally.
Nagagawa mo pa rin ang routine. Nakakangiti ka pa rin. Nakakapag-post ka pa rin. Nakakapag-serve ka pa rin.
Pero sa totoo lang… pagod ka na.
Pagod nang magpanggap. Pagod nang magdala ng invisible burdens. Pagod nang maging “strong” para sa lahat.
Ipinapaalala ng kuwento ni Rachel: Nakikita ng Diyos ang mga pagod na tao.
Hindi lang ang successful. Hindi lang ang mukhang okay.
Nakikita Niya ang mga basag ang puso.
Psalm 34:18:
“The Lord is near unto them that are of a broken heart.”
Ang Hebrew word:
נִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב (Nishberei-lev)
Ibig sabihin: basag, durog, crushed internally.
Lumalapit ang Diyos sa mga sugatang tao.
Hindi Siya lumalayo.
At kung pakiramdam mo lately nauubos ka na emotionally… pakinggan mo ito:
Hindi ka mahina dahil nahirapan ka.
Maging ang mga tapat na tao umiiyak. Maging ang mga obedient na tao napapagod. Maging ang mga chosen na tao minsang bumabagsak emotionally.
Tragic ang pagkamatay ni Rachel.
Pero hindi ito meaningless.
Dahil pagkalipas ng maraming taon… may isa pang Anak na darating sa pamamagitan ng isang masakit ding journey.
Si Jesucristo.
At hindi tulad ni Rachel, kusang pinasok ni Jesus ang kamatayan para mabuhay ang iba.
Ang krus ay hindi aksidente.
Pag-ibig itong sumalo ng hatol. Biyayang sumalo ng kasalanan. Awa na pumasok sa paghihirap.
Sa Aramaic, isa sa mga sigaw ni Jesus sa krus:
ܐܝܠ ܐܝܠ ܠܡܢܐ ܫܒܩܬܢܝ (Eli, Eli, lama shbaqtani)
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Pinasok ni Jesus ang pinakamalalim na anguish ng tao.
Kaya walang sugatang believer ang makakapagsabing: “Hindi naiintindihan ng Diyos ang sakit ko.”
Naiintindihan Niya.
At dahil Siya ay nabuhay muli… hindi pain ang final chapter ng mga kay Cristo.
Iyon ang bulong ng pag-asa sa kuwento ni Rachel.
Masakit ang daan.
Pero totoo pa rin ang resurrection.
Maging honest. Mas tumama ito kaysa inaasahan mo.
May mga taong tuloy pa ring naglalakad habang tahimik na dumudugo sa loob.
